hook.line: Someone says Tomás signed a paper, and he honestly cannot remember it. To talk about your own memory, doubt or certainty, Spanish skips the extra clause and goes straight to *haber*.

examples.es: Estoy segura de haber cerrado la puerta.
examples.en: I'm sure I closed the door. (a woman speaking)
I seem to remember reading something.

examples.es: Creo haber visto a Vale en la calle.
examples.en: I think I saw Vale in the street.

examples.es: Estoy seguro de no haber dejado el celular aquí.
examples.en: I'm sure I didn't leave my phone here. (a man speaking)

examples.es: Hernando asegura haber manejado un taxi durante cuarenta años.
examples.en: Hernando claims to have driven a taxi for forty years.

rule:
When the person who remembers, doubts or feels sure is the same person who did the thing, Spanish skips the clause with *que*. It uses *haber* plus the *-do* form: *No recuerdo haber firmado eso*, not *no recuerdo que yo firmé*.

It works with *recordar*, *creer*, *asegurar* and *me suena*. After adjectives like *seguro* you need *de*: *estoy segura de haber cerrado*.

Different person? Back to *que*: *Recuerdo que Vale cerró la puerta*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a same-subject infinitive clause: when both verbs share a subject, the second becomes an infinitive.

options: I don't remember if I'll sign that.
I won't sign that.
I don't remember signing that.

readAndPick.es: Estoy segura de haber cerrado la puerta.
options: I'm sure I closed the door.
I'm sure I will close the door.
I'm sure she closed the door.
It sounds like I will read something.
I seem to remember reading something.
I seem to remember writing something.

readAndPick.es: Creo haber visto a Vale en la calle.
options: I think I'll see Vale in the street.
I think Vale saw me in the street.
I think I saw Vale in the street.

readAndPick.es: Hernando asegura haber manejado un taxi durante cuarenta años.
options: Hernando claims to have driven a taxi for forty years.
Hernando claims he will drive a taxi for forty years.
Hernando claims I drove a taxi for forty years.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *haber* or *que* and type the whole sentence: *No recuerdo ___ firmado eso.* (I don't remember signing that.)
yourTurn.why: Same person remembers and signed, so no clause: *haber* plus *-do*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm sure I closed the door. (a woman speaking)
yourTurn.answer: Estoy segura de haber cerrado la puerta.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I think I saw Vale in the street.
yourTurn.answer: Creo haber visto a Vale en la calle.
yourTurn.why: *Creo* goes straight to *haber visto*, with no *que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I seem to remember reading something.
yourTurn.why: *Me suena* is followed by *haber* plus the *-do* form.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Recuerdo haber visto ese cartel.* Say: I don't remember seeing that poster.
yourTurn.answer: No recuerdo haber visto ese cartel.
yourTurn.why: Put *no* before *recuerdo*; *haber visto* stays the same.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm sure I didn't leave my phone here. (a man speaking)
yourTurn.answer: Estoy seguro de no haber dejado el celular aquí.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I don't remember calling Mariana.
yourTurn.answer: No recuerdo haber llamado a Mariana.
yourTurn.why: Same frame: *no recuerdo haber* plus the *-do* form.

pitfalls.wrong: No recuerdo que yo firmé eso.
pitfalls.why: Almost. When the same person did it, Spanish skips the *que* clause and uses *haber*.

pitfalls.wrong: Estoy segura haber cerrado la puerta.
pitfalls.right: Estoy segura de haber cerrado la puerta.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *haber*, the verb takes its *-do* ending: *firmado*.

personal: Say one thing you are sure you did, or don't remember doing, with *Estoy seguro de haber* or *No recuerdo haber*.
